findings.description: FAIL, and it is the only finding that blocks this verdict. The r3 fix to the terminal boundary reintroduced the defect r2 closed, and it now puts the clause's check in direct contradiction with the clause's own text. The text says a scenario's three parts must appear 'before the next scenario heading' (:18). The check says 'extract only the text between heading N and the next heading of any level' (:19). Those agree only for a document whose scenarios contain no internal headings. Nothing in the constitution forbids internal headings, and C-4 pushes toward them: each scenario must carry a fixture, a verbatim prompt, a pass-condition table, and a named per-scenario baseline expectation — four blocks, which a worker may well organize under `#### Prompt` / `#### Baseline` / `#### Pass conditions`. Under the check as written, that document's slice for scenario N ends at `#### Prompt`, the table falls outside it, and the emphatic next sentence — 'Anything found outside the slice under test does not count toward it' — instructs the checker to discount it. The result is a FAIL against correct work on a blocker clause, which under the retry ladder burns budget on a worker who did nothing wrong. This is the harm class the clause exists to prevent, arriving through the boundary rule rather than through borrowing. r3 prescribed keeping the heading-N-to-heading-N+1 enumeration and adding only a terminal case; the revision replaced the whole rule instead. Fix, one phrase: 'between heading N and the next scenario heading — or, for the last scenario, `## Grading`'. That keeps r3's terminal boundary and restores r2's subheading immunity in the same breath.

findings.description: Answering the standing question. Both of last round's over-specified clauses came down, and neither lost anything. C-7 dropped the row-by-row signal extraction and the two-stage resolution for a whole-reference read, and it still catches the failure its own example names. The anti-triviality requirement went with it, which is the right trade — it was buying a marginally harder project case at the cost of an unsatisfiable journal one. C-10 kept all four conjuncts; the one I flagged is still there, and 'it writes nothing outside the scratch directory' is still the conjunct a checker has no instrument for and that `git status --porcelain` already covers. That is the only cut I would still make. Nothing new has grown heavier than the failure it prevents. The load has shifted rather than risen: eleven judgment checks against two script checks, and four of the eleven require the checker to execute something — the migrator, the staging script, a tree diff, and a rubric load. I ran all four this round and all four work on this machine, with `yq` present, the humanizer skill resolving, and both executions leaving the tree clean, so Phase 2 should not produce blocked verdicts on infrastructure. What I would still watch is the shape that produced three of last round's six failures and one of this round's: a clause whose judgment is sound and whose procedure is stated one notch off. The countermeasure worked where it was applied — C-6 now points at SKILL.md:122 and C-9 at lint-scope.sh:218-230, and both are correct for the first time in four rounds. C-2 is the clause where a procedure was rewritten from scratch instead, and it is the one that failed.

findings.description: The plain answer you asked for: this is converging, and it is nearly done. r3 carried six failures, four of them on clauses that would have failed correct work. r4 carries one, and it is a four-word edit. Every other clause I re-derived from the skill and the scripts rather than from the priors, and the revisions closed what they were meant to close — C-6 and C-9 in particular were applied rather than cited, which was the specific thing you asked me to distinguish. What is left after C-2 is a list of residuals I would fix in a passing document and would not hold one for: C-7's second-project-directory phrasing, C-9's unowned promotion forms, C-10's check not testing its own new sentence, C-13's dash-form bullets, and the non-goals' external side effect. Each of those is the kind a competent checker rules on correctly by reading the clause text, which is why none of them is a finding. C-2 is not that kind. Its check contradicts its text, so a checker has no tiebreak inside the clause and the two readings produce opposite verdicts on the same correct document. Fix C-2's boundary phrase and I expect r5 to pass; I would not expect a sixth round to find anything at this severity, because the remaining surface is residuals rather than defects.
